# Block 10: Checking the statistics, and reporting the results {.unnumbered} Earlier blocks checked that code runs, that data are clean, and that a refactor leaves results unchanged. None of those checks asks whether the *statistical* code estimates what you think it estimates. This block covers four checks for that, each built on the same division of labour: | You own | The AI writes | The independent check | |---|---|---| | The data-generating mechanism, in words | Simulation and model code | Does the model recover the truth you set? | | The original code and its output | A translation | Do both versions give the same output? | | The pre-registered primary analysis | A list of alternative specifications | Which alternatives are defensible, and do conclusions survive them? | | The numbers in your report | Text around inline code | Is any number typed rather than computed? | *⏱ ~70 minutes* ## Part A: Simulation and parameter recovery *⏱ ~25 minutes* If you simulate data from a mechanism whose parameters you chose, a correct analysis should recover those parameters on average, and its 95% confidence intervals should contain the true values about 95% of the time. This tests the analysis code against a known answer, which real data never provide. Morris, White and Crowther (2019) give a structure for planning simulation studies: the **aims**, the **data-generating mechanism**, the **estimand**, the **methods** and the **performance measures** (ADEMP). Here: - **Aim:** check that the analysis code estimates the high-dose effect correctly. - **Data-generating mechanism:** 12 voles per arm-by-sex cell. Pre-treatment mass is normal with mean 28 g and SD 2 g. Post-treatment mass equals 2.8 g plus 0.9 times pre-treatment mass, plus 0.8 g for Low_dose, plus 1.5 g for High_dose, plus 1.0 g for males, plus normal error with SD 0.8 g. - **Estimand:** the difference in post-treatment mass between High_dose and Control, adjusted for pre-treatment mass and sex. True value: 1.5 g. - **Method:** linear model (ANCOVA), `mass_post_g ~ mass_pre_g + treatment_arm + sex`. - **Performance measures:** bias and confidence-interval coverage, each with its Monte Carlo standard error. The written mechanism is yours. It is the equivalent of the codebook in the [data-cleaning block](11g-data-cleaning.qmd): the AI turns it into code, and you check the code against it. :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} Write, check, recover (25 minutes) :::: ::::{.task-container} **1. Simulation code.** Give the AI the data-generating mechanism above, word for word, and ask for a function `simulate_voles()` returning a tibble with columns `treatment_arm`, `sex`, `mass_pre_g` and `mass_post_g`. **2. Check the simulated data against the specification.** Before using the function, run it once and check that it matches what you wrote: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(1) sim_df <- simulate_voles() sim_df |> count(treatment_arm, sex) # 12 per cell? sim_df |> summarise(mean(mass_pre_g), sd(mass_pre_g)) sim_df |> summarise(mean_post = mean(mass_post_g), .by = c(treatment_arm, sex)) ``` ::: High_dose should be about 1.5 g above Control within each sex, and males about 1 g above females. If not, the simulation is wrong, and nothing built on it can be trusted. **3. Analysis code, in a separate session.** Without showing it the simulation code, ask the AI for a function `estimate_high_vs_control(data)` that fits the model above and returns the High_dose estimate and its 95% confidence interval. **4. Run the recovery.**
::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} simulate_voles <- function(n_per_cell = 12, effect_low = 0.8, effect_high = 1.5, sex_effect = 1.0, slope_pre = 0.9, sd_pre = 2, sd_resid = 0.8) { tidyr::expand_grid( treatment_arm = c("Control", "Low_dose", "High_dose"), sex = c("F", "M"), animal = seq_len(n_per_cell) ) |> dplyr::mutate( mass_pre_g = stats::rnorm(dplyr::n(), mean = 28, sd = sd_pre), arm_effect = dplyr::case_when( treatment_arm == "Low_dose" ~ effect_low, treatment_arm == "High_dose" ~ effect_high, .default = 0 ), mass_post_g = 28 * (1 - slope_pre) + slope_pre * mass_pre_g + arm_effect + sex_effect * (sex == "M") + stats::rnorm(dplyr::n(), sd = sd_resid) ) |> dplyr::select(treatment_arm, sex, mass_pre_g, mass_post_g) } estimate_high_vs_control <- function(data) { data <- dplyr::mutate( data, treatment_arm = factor(treatment_arm, levels = c("Control", "Low_dose", "High_dose")) ) fit <- stats::lm(mass_post_g ~ mass_pre_g + treatment_arm + sex, data = data) ci <- stats::confint(fit)["treatment_armHigh_dose", ] tibble::tibble( estimate = unname(stats::coef(fit)["treatment_armHigh_dose"]), lower = unname(ci[1]), upper = unname(ci[2]) ) } ``` :::
::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(2026) n_sim <- 1000 true_effect <- 1.5 results_df <- seq_len(n_sim) |> map(\(i) estimate_high_vs_control(simulate_voles(effect_high = true_effect))) |> list_rbind() results_df |> summarise( bias = mean(estimate) - true_effect, bias_mcse = sd(estimate) / sqrt(n_sim), coverage = mean(lower <= true_effect & upper >= true_effect), coverage_mcse = sqrt(coverage * (1 - coverage) / n_sim), empirical_se = sd(estimate) ) ``` ::: Bias should be within about two Monte Carlo standard errors of zero. Coverage should be within about two Monte Carlo standard errors of 0.95, roughly 0.936 to 0.964 with 1,000 runs. **5. Prove the check can fail.** Replace the analysis with a version that models the change the wrong way round, as in the [debugging block](11c-debugging.qmd): ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} estimate_buggy <- function(data) { data <- dplyr::mutate( data, treatment_arm = factor(treatment_arm, levels = c("Control", "Low_dose", "High_dose")), mass_change_g = mass_pre_g - mass_post_g ) fit <- stats::lm(mass_change_g ~ treatment_arm + sex, data = data) ci <- stats::confint(fit)["treatment_armHigh_dose", ] tibble::tibble( estimate = unname(stats::coef(fit)["treatment_armHigh_dose"]), lower = unname(ci[1]), upper = unname(ci[2]) ) } ``` ::: Rerun the recovery with `estimate_buggy()`. Bias should be about −3 g and coverage near zero. A check you have never seen fail is a check you are assuming works. :::: ::: :::{.callout-warning} **What recovery does not prove.** It shows that the code estimates the right quantity *under the mechanism you simulated*. It says nothing about whether real voles behave like that. A change-score model fitted to these simulated data would also be nearly unbiased (randomisation makes both estimators valid), but less precise; compare `empirical_se` to see the cost. Recovery tests code, not scientific assumptions. ::: ## Part B: Translation with an equivalence check *⏱ ~15 minutes* Translating code (base R to tidyverse, or SPSS, Stata or SAS to R) is a task AI does quickly. The characterisation-test idea applies directly: run both versions and compare the outputs. :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} Translate and compare (15 minutes) :::: ::::{.task-container} **1.** Here is a short base R script: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} voles <- read.csv(here::here("data", "raw", "voles_metabolism.csv"), stringsAsFactors = TRUE) rate_mean <- aggregate(metabolic_rate_post ~ treatment_arm + sex, data = voles, FUN = mean) rate_n <- aggregate(metabolic_rate_post ~ treatment_arm + sex, data = voles, FUN = length) names(rate_n)[3] <- "n" legacy_summary <- merge(rate_mean, rate_n, by = c("treatment_arm", "sex")) ``` ::: **2.** Ask the AI to translate it into tidyverse code producing `tidy_summary`, with the same columns. **3.** Compare. Normalise only *presentation* (type and row order), never values: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} normalise <- function(data) { data |> as_tibble() |> mutate(across(where(is.factor), as.character)) |> arrange(treatment_arm, sex) } testthat::expect_equal(normalise(tidy_summary), normalise(legacy_summary)) ``` ::: **4.** If the comparison fails after normalising, you have found a real difference in behaviour. Find it before reading on.
`aggregate()` with a formula drops rows with a missing value in any variable in the formula, silently. The one animal with no `metabolic_rate_post` is excluded from both the mean and the count. A direct translation using `summarise(mean(metabolic_rate_post), n())` returns `NA` for that cell's mean and counts the animal in `n`. Neither version is "the translation"; they make different decisions about missing data. Decide which you want, write it explicitly (`na.rm = TRUE` and a count of non-missing values), and record the decision. This is the same problem as the "unchanged is not correct" step of the [characterisation-test block](11i-characterisation-tests.qmd), reached from a different direction.
:::: ::: When translating from other software, you usually cannot run the original inside R. Export its results to a file, compare against those, and expect differences in defaults: how missing values are handled, how quantiles are defined, and how results are rounded. Each difference needs a decision, not a tolerance setting. ## Part C: Robustness, not choice *⏱ ~15 minutes* AI should not choose your primary analysis. The BLADE benchmark compared language-model agents with expert analysts on open-ended research questions. It found that the models were often limited to basic analyses, and that agents able to explore the data made more varied but still sub-optimal analytical decisions (Gu et al., 2024). Its useful role is narrower: listing defensible alternatives to an analysis you have already fixed, so you can check whether your conclusion depends on the choice. :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} Enumerate, judge, run (15 minutes) :::: ::::{.task-container} **1. Ask for alternatives, not a recommendation:** ``` My pre-registered primary analysis is an ANCOVA: mass_post_g ~ mass_pre_g + treatment_arm + sex, estimating the High_dose versus Control difference. List alternative specifications a reasonable analyst might use for the same question, and for each, say whether it estimates the same quantity. Do not recommend one. ``` **2. Judge each one yourself.** Mark it defensible or not, with a reason. Check especially whether the alternative estimates the *same* quantity. **3. Run the defensible ones and report them beside the primary analysis.** ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} voles_df <- read_csv(here("data", "raw", "voles_metabolism.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) |> mutate(treatment_arm = factor(treatment_arm, levels = c("Control", "Low_dose", "High_dose"))) specs_df <- tribble( ~spec, ~formula, "Primary: ANCOVA", "mass_post_g ~ mass_pre_g + treatment_arm + sex", "Change score", "I(mass_post_g - mass_pre_g) ~ treatment_arm + sex", "ANCOVA with arm-by-sex", "mass_post_g ~ mass_pre_g + treatment_arm * sex" ) spec_results_df <- specs_df |> mutate(result = map(formula, \(f) { fit <- lm(as.formula(f), data = voles_df) ci <- confint(fit)["treatment_armHigh_dose", ] tibble( estimate = unname(coef(fit)["treatment_armHigh_dose"]), lower = unname(ci[1]), upper = unname(ci[2]) ) })) |> unnest(result) spec_results_df ``` :::
In the third specification, the coefficient `treatment_armHigh_dose` is the High_dose effect **in females only** (the reference level of `sex`), because the model includes an interaction. It sits in the same column as the other estimates but answers a different question. It belongs in a separate analysis of whether the effect differs by sex, not in a table of estimates of the same quantity. An AI that lists it as an "alternative" without saying so has made exactly the error step 2 asks you to catch.
:::: ::: :::{.callout-warning} Running many specifications and reporting the one you like best is selective reporting. The primary analysis is fixed in advance; the others are reported as sensitivity analyses whatever they show. ::: ## Part D: Reporting without typed numbers *⏱ ~10 minutes* A number typed into a report is a number that can be mistyped, or left unchanged when the data change. When an assistant drafts the text, it may also "helpfully" restate numbers it saw earlier in the conversation. Every number in the prose should come from inline code: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # in a chunk primary <- spec_results_df |> filter(spec == "Primary: ANCOVA") ``` ::: and in the text: ``` High-dose voles were `r round(primary$estimate, 2)` g heavier than controls after treatment (95% CI `r round(primary$lower, 2)` to `r round(primary$upper, 2)` g). ``` Your `AGENTS.md` should already say never to type numerical results into text. That is a request. This function is the check: it lists prose lines in a `.qmd` file that still contain numbers outside inline code, for you to review by eye. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} find_typed_numbers <- function(path) { lines <- readLines(path, warn = FALSE) is_fence <- grepl("^```", lines) in_chunk <- cumsum(is_fence) %% 2 == 1 tibble(line = seq_along(lines), text = lines) |> filter(!in_chunk, !is_fence) |> mutate(prose = gsub("`\\{?r\\}? [^`]*`", "", text)) |> filter(grepl("[0-9]+\\.[0-9]+|\\b[0-9]{2,}\\b", prose, perl = TRUE)) |> select(line, text) } find_typed_numbers(here("report.qmd")) ``` ::: It will also flag years, sample sizes from the design and the YAML header, so treat each hit as a question, not an error. **Record AI use as you go.** Many journals, funders and institutions now ask authors to declare AI use. A short log written at the time is easier and more accurate than reconstruction later. One line per session is enough: ``` 2026-10-09; Claude Code (model as reported in the session); translated summary script to tidyverse; kept translation, changed missing-value handling to na.rm = TRUE after equivalence check. ``` Check your institution's and target journal's current policy for what must be declared and where. ## Check your understanding **A simulation recovers the true effect with negligible bias and 95% coverage. What has it shown?**
**A translated script and the original disagree only after you convert factors to characters and sort the rows. What should you do next?**
**Why should the arm-by-sex interaction model not appear in the same robustness table as the primary ANCOVA?**
## References - Gu, K., Shang, R., Jiang, R., et al. (2024). BLADE: Benchmarking language model agents for data-driven science. In *Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2024*, 13936–13971. - Morris, T.P., White, I.R. and Crowther, M.J. (2019). Using simulation studies to evaluate statistical methods. *Statistics in Medicine*, 38(11), 2074–2102.
